summary: Strait of Belle Isle light near Port au Choix, first lit in 1871; burned in 1890; the present wooden tower dates from 1892; keepers included the Breton family.

structures.type: octagonal wooden tower with lantern and gallery, red lantern (the register says hexagonal)
hexagonal tower with catoptric light; buildings completed 1870

structures.status: burned; foundation remains (LF dates the fire to 1998 in its text)

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed; reached by road or on foot by Philip's Garden Coastal Trail (LF, Rowlett).

facts.agency: Canadian Coast Guard (owner); Parks Canada, Port au Choix National Historic Site (site manager)

white flash every fifteen seconds, first shown 26 August 1871

corrections.why: The standing wooden tower was built in 1892, after the first tower burned in 1890. The 1871 date belongs to the first tower, which the record lists as the standing structure.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Both dates are right for different things. The station was first lit on 26 August 1871 (LF; Rowlett 'station established 1871'). The present tower was built in 1892 and first lit on 20 October 1892 (LF; register, Rowlett). Wikidata's 1892 is the present tower's first light.

notes_for_editor: 1) Tower plan: the federal register (historicplaces and the Heritage Guide copy) describes a hexagonal tower; the Coast Guard list, Rowlett and LF say octagonal. The story reports both and follows the three octagonal sources in 'Today'. 2) Height: the record's 19.8 m (Wikidata) against Rowlett's 19 m (63 ft); LF gives 58 ft from base to vane for the 1892 tower. Not corrected. 3) Lens: LF calls the 1908 optic a third-order Fresnel lens; the 1909 Department report calls it a third-order dioptric. The record has no lens; facts use dioptric per the Department. 4) Keepers: LF lists Narcisse Breton (1896-1926), then 'Joseph N. Romeo Breton' (1926-27) and 'Joseph Narcisse Gaudias Breton' (1927-59) as separate entries. They may be one family or two men; LF does not say. Not merged. 5) The 1901 keepers' table (scan p.255, printed p.144) is OCR; 'Breton, Narcisse' sits on the same printed line as Point Rich. The page image was checked on 2026-10-27 (IA viewer, scan p.255) and confirms the line. 6) The 1902 Meteorological passage (scan p.191, printed p.14) names six stations inspected by H. V. Payne. Point Rich is named in that paragraph among the stations Payne inspected, as the story says; the sixth station is cut off in the OCR text read, so the sixth is not named. 7) The 1905 Marconi passage is about a wireless station, not the light; the story says so. 8) The 1923-24 report (fiscal 1922-23) lists two power sets from 'the Point Riche and Cape Ray Stations' installed at Point Amour; the same paragraph mentions a new earth system and aerial, and the 1905 report lists Point Rich and Cape Ray among the Marconi wireless stations. The story now says the report does not say which kind of station it means, and that these were probably wireless stations. 9) LF dates the keeper's house fire to 'the 1998' in its text, which is probably a typo for an earlier date. The story gives LF's date with a note. 10) Source gaps: the 1874 Barbour narrative, 1876 wrecks, 1877-79 fog horn and the 1890 fire come from LF (which cites the Department's reports and the New York Times). The 1874-1879 Department reports are not in the local corpus. Chronicling America searches for 1890 returned French Shore pieces only, not the fire report, so the fire rests on LF and Rowlett. 11) Privacy: the Breton family and Rumbolt are named only as LF prints them in keeper roles, with no personal details. The story gives no family details. 12) Wikipedia was used only as a lead and is not cited (its keeper and tower data were not needed).
